<reflection>
- The first experiment resulted in very similar NLL values (around -23.5 to -23.9) for the majority of the models (M1, M2, M7, M9-M20). This indicates that a standard reaction condition (S=2.0, cat=0.05, P=0.0) does not provide enough information to distinguish between standard Michaelis-Menten, various deactivation pathways, and product/substrate inhibition.
- The aim of establishing a baseline was achieved, as we can now confidently rule out M3, M4, and M5, but we need more targeted conditions to break the degeneracy among the remaining models.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To differentiate the remaining models, we need to amplify the specific conditions that trigger their unique pathways. 
First, by introducing a maximum initial product concentration (P=0.5), we can strongly isolate mechanisms involving product-induced deactivation (M12, M17). 
Second, by increasing the catalyst concentration to its maximum (0.20, a 4-fold increase), we will dramatically amplify the rates of bimolecular catalyst interactions (M2, M13, M18, M19), which scale with the square of the catalyst species concentration. 
Finally, lowering the substrate concentration to 1.0 (compared to 2.0 in the first run) reduces the S/cat ratio from 40 to 5. This will significantly increase the proportion of free catalyst (`cat`) relative to the catalyst-substrate complex (`catS`), helping to distinguish whether deactivation or inhibition occurs via the free catalyst (M9, M11, M12, M13) or the bound complex (M14, M16, M17, M18). 
This single experiment simultaneously probes product effects, bimolecular catalyst interactions, and shifts the catalyst resting state, maximizing information gain across the entire set of plausible mechanisms.
</hypothesis>
